title: Extended localization Cech complex computes derived ideal-power torsion
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $r\geq0$ and $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in R$, put $K=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)$, and let $M$ be any $R$-module, not necessarily finitely generated. Let $\Gamma_K$ be the ideal-power torsion functor [def-sbc-ideal-power-torsion-functor], so $\Gamma_K(M)=\{m:K^nm=0\text{ for some }n\geq1\}$, and set $H_K^q(M)=R^q\Gamma_K(M)$ for $q\geq0$.

For $t\in R$, write $M_t$ for localization at the powers of $t$: its fractions $m/t^a$ satisfy $m/t^a=m'/t^b$ exactly when $t^c(t^b m-t^a m')=0$ for some $c\geq0$. Define the extended alternating cochain complex $C_R(t_1,\ldots,t_r;M)$ by
$$C^0=M,\qquad C^p=\prod_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_p\leq r}M_{t_{i_1}\cdots t_{i_p}}\quad(1\leq p\leq r),$$
and $C^p=0$ outside $0\leq p\leq r$. The degree-zero differential sends $m$ to $(m/1)_i$. For $p\geq1$, the component of $d^p(x)$ indexed by $i_1<\cdots<i_{p+1}$ is $\sum_{a=1}^{p+1}(-1)^{a-1}x_{i_1\ldots\widehat{i_a}\ldots i_{p+1}}$, with each summand mapped to the indicated localization. These are cochain differentials. If $r=0$ the complex is $M$ in degree zero only. For every $q\geq0$ there is a natural $R$-linear isomorphism
$$H_K^q(M)\cong H^q(C_R(t_1,\ldots,t_r;M)),$$
where $H^q(C)=\ker(d^q)/\operatorname{im}(d^{q-1})$, with the incoming image zero in degree zero.

source.place: Tag 0956 (lemma-compute-local-cohomology-noetherian), the module assertion and the displayed extended alternating localization complex.

proof.text: The displayed maps are $R$-linear. In a component indexed by $i_1<\cdots<i_{p+2}$, each term of $d^{p+1}d^p$ comes from deleting a pair of indices. If their positions are $a<b$, deleting $b$ then $a$ has coefficient $(-1)^{b-1+a-1}$, whereas deleting $a$ then the new position $b-1$ has coefficient $(-1)^{a-1+b-2}$. These sum to zero, and the two localization maps agree on every fraction. This includes the composite starting at degree zero: its two terms are $m/1-m/1$. At the end of the complex the target is zero. Thus $d^{p+1}d^p=0$. A module map acts on each fraction by $m/u\mapsto f(m)/u$; the fraction relation makes this well-defined and the same formula shows it commutes with every differential.

source.place: Tag 0956 (lemma-compute-local-cohomology-noetherian), module assertion and the displayed extended alternating localization complex.

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-local-cohomology-cech-bound] with $A=R$, $f_i=t_i$, $I=K$ and $j=q$. Its hypotheses require precisely a commutative Noetherian ring, a finite list of generators and an arbitrary module; all are present, and neither nonzeroness of $R$, properness of $K$, nor finite generation of $M$ is required. Its $C^0=M$, its degree-$p$ products indexed by increasing $p$-tuples, its degree-zero localization map, its signs $(-1)^{a-1}$, and its zero terms outside degrees $0,\ldots,r$ are exactly those of the complex in this statement. The localization $M_g$ in that node is at the powers of $g$, exactly as specified here by the fraction relation. The torsion convention agrees with [def-sbc-ideal-power-torsion-functor]: allowing exponent zero adds only the element zero, which is already killed by $K^1$. Consequently the cited natural $R$-linear comparison is an isomorphism $a_M:H^q(C_R(t_1,\ldots,t_r;M))\longrightarrow H_K^q(M)$.

source.place: Tag 0956 (lemma-compute-local-cohomology-noetherian), module assertion and the displayed extended alternating localization complex.

proof.text: Take $a_M^{-1}$ to obtain the stated direction. For an $R$-linear map $f:M\to N$, naturality of Step 2 says $H_K^q(f)a_M=a_N H^q(C_R(t;f))$. Multiplying on the left by $a_N^{-1}$ and on the right by $a_M^{-1}$ gives $a_N^{-1}H_K^q(f)=H^q(C_R(t;f))a_M^{-1}$, proving naturality in the required direction. The inverse is $R$-linear: applying the injective map $a_M$ to the addition and scalar-multiplication identities reduces them to linearity of $a_M$. For $r=0$ the cited comparison explicitly uses $K=(0)$ and the complex $M$ in degree zero, so the same conclusion covers $q=0$ and all higher degrees without a nonempty-list assumption.
